I am 60 years old and have farmed my whole life here in Quzhou County on the North China Plain. I know every inch of my 6 *mu* of flat land, and I have learned that you do not gamble with unfamiliar crops when your family’s livelihood depends on it. The wheat-maize double-cropping system is what this soil and climate were made for, and the government still guarantees purchase of wheat, so that is my anchor. I will sow improved winter wheat varieties in late October—seeds I buy from the county supply store, the same ones my neighbors trust. After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant improved summer maize; the window between harvests is narrow, so I use rotary tillage to save time and labor. For wheat, I apply plenty of nitrogen because spring drought always hits and the crop needs vigor; I irrigate four times, especially at jointing and grain-filling. Maize gets less irrigation—twice is usually enough with the summer rains—and I spray pesticides two or three times for each crop to control the borers and rust we see every year. I keep my input costs moderate; I am too old to chase speculative profits, but I know how to get steady yields from this land.
